title: How Much Does a Trip to Korea Cost? A Daily and Weekly Budget Breakdown
html:
"How much should I budget for Korea?" is one of the hardest questions to answer with a single number, because Korea can genuinely be a $50-a-day destination or a $300-a-day destination depending on how you travel — the country itself doesn't set the price, your choices do. Below is a realistic breakdown for three travel styles, plus the individual costs (subway rides, meals, hotel nights) that make up those totals, all based on current 2026 prices.

Backpacker Budget: ₩70,000–100,000 ($50–75) a Day

This is the "see everything, spend carefully" style — hostel dorms, convenience store meals and street food, and getting everywhere on public transit.

  • Accommodation: a bed in a hostel dorm in Hongdae, Myeongdong, or Jongno runs about ₩25,000–45,000 a night.
  • Food: a convenience store dosirak (도시락, a pre-packed lunch box you microwave in-store) costs ₩5,000–7,000, and a street food snack at a market stall is usually under ₩5,000. Two or three of these a day comes to roughly ₩15,000–25,000.
  • Transport: a single subway or bus ride with a T-money card (Korea's rechargeable transit card, sold for ₩2,500–4,000 at any convenience store) costs ₩1,550, with a discount if you transfer within the free-transfer window. Budget ₩5,000–8,000 a day for getting around.
  • Activities: most of Seoul's best sights — palace grounds from outside, neighborhoods like Bukchon and Ikseon-dong, markets, parks, the Han River — cost nothing to walk around. A palace ticket (like Gyeongbokgung) is only ₩3,000 for adults 19–64, and free for visitors 18 and under or 65 and over.

Locals eat this way too on an ordinary workday — plenty of Korean office workers grab a dosirak or a quick bowl of noodles for lunch instead of a full sit-down meal, so you won't stand out for keeping food costs low.

Convenience stores like CU, GS25, and 7-Eleven are everywhere in Seoul and are where budget travelers get a lot of their meals. Photo by LERK, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Mid-Range Budget: ₩140,000–220,000 ($100–160) a Day

This is the most common style for first-time visitors — a comfortable hotel room, a real sit-down meal at least once a day, and the occasional taxi when your feet are tired.

  • Accommodation: a clean budget-to-mid business hotel or a private guesthouse room runs about ₩80,000–150,000 a night.
  • Food: a sit-down Korean meal — bibimbap, a bowl of noodles, Korean BBQ for one — costs around ₩12,000–25,000 per person, and a cafe coffee is roughly ₩4,500–6,000. Mixing a couple of restaurant meals with a convenience store breakfast keeps this closer to ₩45,000–60,000 a day.
  • Transport: mostly T-money subway and bus rides, with an occasional taxi. A Seoul taxi starts at ₩4,800 for the first 1.6 km, so a short cross-town ride is usually ₩8,000–15,000 — just note that fares rise 20–40% between 10 pm and 4 am.
  • Activities: one paid experience a day — a palace with a hanbok rental, a cooking class, a museum, a DMZ or Nami Island day tour — typically adds ₩15,000–60,000.

Sit-down restaurants are also where you'll notice Korea's tipping culture is simply absent — the price on the menu is the price you pay, no extra math needed.

A traditional Korean restaurant in Insadong — the kind of sit-down meal that becomes a regular part of your day once you move past a strict backpacker budget. Photo by Julie, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Comfortable & Luxury Budget: ₩280,000+ ($200+) a Day

If you'd rather not think about small costs at all, this tier covers a nicer hotel, restaurant meals without checking the price first, and taxis instead of transfers.

  • Accommodation: a 4- or 5-star hotel in central Seoul (Myeongdong, Gangnam, or near the Han River) typically runs ₩250,000–500,000+ a night.
  • Food: fine dining, hotel restaurants, and higher-end Korean BBQ or omakase easily run ₩50,000–150,000+ per meal.
  • Transport: taxis for most trips, or a private driver for day trips outside the city.
  • Activities: private guided tours, spa and jjimjilbang (Korean sauna) premium packages, and shopping add up quickly here — this is the tier where the budget is really a matter of personal taste rather than necessity.

Even at this level, it's worth keeping a T-money card in your wallet — Seoul's subway is genuinely one of the fastest ways to cross the city during rush hour, and plenty of well-off locals use it for exactly that reason.

A city view like this is often part of what you're paying for at a higher-end Seoul hotel. Photo by Takipoint123, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

A few easy ways to stretch your budget, whatever tier you're in:

  • Load a T-money card once and reuse it for subway, bus, convenience stores, and even some taxis — it's cheaper than single-journey paper tickets every time.
  • Many palaces are free on the last Wednesday of the month ("Culture Day"), and free year-round if you're wearing a proper hanbok.
  • Convenience store meal deals (look for yellow discount stickers, usually in the evening) can cut a dosirak's price in half.
  • Weekday hotel rates are often noticeably lower than Friday–Saturday rates — shifting a booking by even one day can save real money.

Quick comparison: daily and weekly budget by travel style

BackpackerMid-RangeComfortable / Luxury
AccommodationHostel dormBusiness hotel / guesthouse4–5 star hotel
FoodConvenience store, street foodSit-down restaurants, cafesFine dining, premium BBQ
TransportSubway / bus onlySubway / bus + occasional taxiTaxis / private driver
Estimated daily total₩70,000–100,000 ($50–75)₩140,000–220,000 ($100–160)₩280,000+ ($200+)
Estimated 7-day total*₩490,000–700,000 (~$360–520)₩980,000–1,540,000 (~$730–1,150)₩1,960,000+ (~$1,450+)

*Excludes international flights. Won-to-dollar figures use an approximate rate of ₩1,350 = $1 (September 2026); check the current rate before you travel, since it shifts from week to week.

💬 Not sure which budget tier fits your trip, or want help estimating costs for a specific itinerary? Ask in the comments — happy to help!
meta_description: A practical 2026 breakdown of daily and weekly Korea travel costs for first-time visitors — hostel to luxury budgets, food, transport, and ways to save money.
